insufficientFunds.title: Insufficient funds
insufficientFunds.reason: Your bank reported that the card doesn't have enough balance to complete this donation.
insufficientFunds.fix: Top up your card, lower the donation amount, or try a different card.

cardDeclined.title: Your bank declined the card
cardDeclined.reason: Your card issuer refused this transaction. This is the bank's call, not ours — they don't always share the exact reason.
cardDeclined.fix: Try another card, or contact your bank to find out why it was blocked.

expiredCard.title: The card has expired
expiredCard.reason: The card you used is past its expiry date. Banks won't process payments on expired cards.
expiredCard.fix: Switch to a valid card. Your bank can issue a replacement if needed.

invalidCvc.title: The security code (CVV) was wrong
invalidCvc.reason: The 3- or 4-digit CVV/CVC didn't match what your bank has on file.
invalidCvc.fix: Double-check the security code on the back of your card and try again.

incorrectNumber.title: The card number looks wrong
incorrectNumber.reason: The card number we sent didn't match a valid card at your bank.
incorrectNumber.fix: Re-enter the 16-digit card number carefully and try again.

lostOrStolen.title: Card reported lost or stolen
lostOrStolen.reason: Your bank flagged this card as lost or stolen and won't allow new payments on it.
lostOrStolen.fix: Contact your bank for a replacement, then try a different card here.

doNotHonor.title: Generic decline by your bank
doNotHonor.reason: Your bank refused the transaction without telling us exactly why. This is often a fraud-prevention block on cross-border donations.
doNotHonor.fix: Call the number on the back of your card and ask them to approve this charity donation, then retry.

limitExceeded.title: Daily or monthly limit reached
limitExceeded.reason: Your card's daily spend limit or transaction count for the month has been exceeded.
limitExceeded.fix: Lower the donation amount, wait until tomorrow, or try a different card.

currencyNotSupported.title: Currency not supported by your card
currencyNotSupported.reason: Your card can't process payments in the donation currency.
currencyNotSupported.fix: Switch the currency from the top-right of the site, or use a card that supports international payments.

authenticationFailed.title: 3-D Secure check failed
authenticationFailed.reason: Your bank's 3-D Secure verification didn't go through. This usually means the SMS/app code was wrong or timed out.
authenticationFailed.fix: Make sure your phone is reachable, then retry. Have the bank's 3DS app ready before you tap retry.

processingError.title: Temporary processing error
processingError.reason: The payment didn't go through, but it's not a problem with your card — something on the bank's side glitched.
processingError.fix: Wait a minute and retry. Most processing errors clear by themselves.

networkError.title: Connection problem
networkError.reason: We couldn't reach the bank to process the payment. This is almost always a transient network issue.
networkError.fix: Check your internet connection, then retry. The exact same card will most likely succeed.

issuerUnavailable.title: Your bank's system is unavailable
issuerUnavailable.reason: Your card issuer's payment system is temporarily down or unreachable.
issuerUnavailable.fix: Wait a few minutes and try again, or use a different card from another bank.

fraudSuspected.title: Blocked as suspected fraud
fraudSuspected.reason: Your bank's fraud system flagged the donation. Charity donations from a new merchant can trigger this — it's a false positive most of the time.
fraudSuspected.fix: Call the number on the back of your card, confirm it's really you, and ask them to whitelist this merchant.

generic.title: Payment didn't go through
generic.reason: Something stopped the payment from completing. We weren't given a specific reason.
generic.fix: Try again, switch to a different card, or use the bank transfer option below.

AboutUs.aboutUsDesc1: Minberiaksa International Solidarity Association began its work in healthcare, most notably by helping to develop the facilities of Haydarpaşa Numune Hospital. In years when Turkey's health system was under strain, the association supported patients of limited means with both their medical examinations and the cost of their medicines. Opened on 9 November 1961 by a group of doctors and nurses, this door of charity has served with pride for more than sixty years.
AboutUs.aboutUsDesc2: In recognition of that sincere and sustained work, the association was granted the status of an “Association Working for the Public Benefit” by Council of Ministers Decision No. 6/2090, dated 10 August 1963. In an age when a war or a natural disaster in one corner of the world can affect us all, our 2023 congress adopted changes to the association's management and statutes that widened our field of work to include natural disasters, emergency relief and educational aid.
AboutUs.visionQuote: To nourish the stomach, the mind and the heart of people everywhere — ensuring that food, truth and wisdom reach all people.
AboutUs.goalsTitle: The Goals We Strive to Achieve
AboutUs.goalsDesc: We stand beside people left destitute by war, natural disaster and terrorism, working to rebuild both their circumstances and their dignity.
AboutUs.ctaDesc: Join us on our journey to build a better future for children around the world.
goalsList: To help people suffering deprivation because of war, natural disaster or terrorism.
To repair the homes of those whose houses have been destroyed or who have lost their livelihood.
To work, materially and spiritually, to build up the human being.
To help those denied education, the most basic of human rights.
To raise upright, well-rounded people both at home and abroad.
To deliver emergency relief quickly and dependably when disaster strikes.
To sustain support in healthcare, the field in which the association was founded.
presidentMessageParagraphs: The door opened in 1961 by a group of doctors and nurses, in the simple hope of doing good, has remained open with that same resolve for more than sixty years.

In our founding years we focused on healthcare: we contributed to developing the facilities of Haydarpaşa Numune Hospital and met the examination and medicine costs of patients who could not afford them.
The status of an “Association Working for the Public Benefit”, granted by Council of Ministers Decision No. 6/2090 of 10 August 1963, was the official recognition of that effort.

We live in an age in which the world has become one large village, and a war or disaster in one region touches everyone. For that reason, our 2023 congress widened our field of work to cover natural disasters, emergency relief and educational aid.
Our aim is not only to meet a need. It is to repair homes, to stand beside those denied an education, and to build up the human being both materially and spiritually.
On this road our greatest support is the trust you place in us and the giving you entrust to our care.

about.heroSubtitle: Minbar Al Aqsa is an international foundation for scholars, orators and preachers, based in Istanbul, Türkiye. It brings them together from around the world to raise awareness of the cause of Bayt al-Maqdis and Al-Aqsa Mosque through various platforms.
about.mission: Working with orators and preachers to build awareness of the cause of Bayt al-Maqdis and to strengthen the steadfastness of its people.
about.howWeWork: We rely on a field team in Al-Quds and Gaza to execute and follow up projects, documenting every stage with photos and reports. We publish no unverified number and describe no undocumented work.
about.vision: The first reference for orators and preachers worldwide in serving the cause of Bayt al-Maqdis.
about.visionDetail: Minbar Al Aqsa is an international foundation for scholars, orators and preachers, based in Istanbul, seeking to gather them from around the world to raise awareness of Bayt al-Maqdis and Al-Aqsa Mosque through various platforms.
about.legalText: A humanitarian foundation officially registered in Türkiye (Minbar Al Aqsa Derneği), based in Istanbul and operating under Turkish charity regulations.
about.objective1: Uniting the efforts of orators and preachers worldwide in serving the cause of Bayt al-Maqdis.
about.objective2: Expanding into available countries and coordinating with relevant bodies to serve the cause of Bayt al-Maqdis.
about.objective3: Preparing orators and preachers to mobilize the Ummah for Bayt al-Maqdis, and providing them a scholarly Maqdisi incubator.
about.objective4: Highlighting orators and preachers devoted to Bayt al-Maqdis as Maqdisi references for the Ummah.
about.objective5: Motivating orators and preachers to rally the Ummah and invest its energies to strengthen the steadfastness of the people of Al-Quds and meet their needs.

about.dept2P2: Providing media material for Maqdisi outreach work
about.dept2P3: Opening media channels to preachers active in serving the cause
about.dept3P1: Promoting direct-aid and Waqf donation projects to serve and protect Al-Quds and its holy sites
about.pillar1Text: Restoring homes, supporting Maqdisi families, and serving Al-Aqsa Mosque and its people.
about.pillar2Text: Urgent food relief: hot meals, parcels, bread and water.
about.pillar3Text: Independent channels for Zakat and Waqf, spent on their approved categories.

aqsa.confusionText: Confining the name "Al-Aqsa" to the Dome of the Rock alone, or to the Qibli Mosque alone, shrinks its boundaries in people's minds. Al-Aqsa is the whole sanctuary: its wall, its courtyards, its prayer halls and its domes.

aqsa.lm1_text: It stands at the center of the raised Rock courtyard above the Noble Rock — an octagonal building topped with a golden dome, its walls faced with blue tiles renewed in the Ottoman era. It is among the oldest Islamic buildings still standing today.
aqsa.lm1_v1: Under Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, completed 72 AH
aqsa.lm1_v2: The Rock courtyard, at the centre of the mosque grounds
aqsa.lm2_text: The large lead-domed building at the southernmost, qibla-facing end of the mosque — the main hall for Friday and congregational prayer. Built in the Umayyad era, and rebuilt in succession by the Umayyads, Abbasids, Fatimids, Ayyubids, Mamluks and Ottomans.
aqsa.lm2_v2: The mihrab, the minbar and Maqam al-Arba'in
aqsa.lm3_text: A vast vaulted hall on massive columns beneath the south-eastern corner of the mosque, part of the levelling that raised the mosque courtyard. It was cleared and prepared for prayer in the 1990s, becoming one of its largest halls.
aqsa.lm3_v1: Below the level of the south-eastern courtyard
aqsa.lm4_slotHint: Image of the Old Aqsa Mosque
aqsa.lm4_text: A vaulted passage and prayer hall extending beneath Al-Qibli, ending at the Double Gate in the southern wall — once an entrance for worshippers before the southern gates were closed.
aqsa.lm4_v1: Leads to the closed Double Gate
aqsa.lm4_v2: Opened for prayer during crowded times
aqsa.lm5_slotHint: Image of the Dome of the Chain
aqsa.lm5_text: A small open dome resting on marble columns directly east of the Dome of the Rock, among the oldest domes still standing in the mosque, used as a prayer spot and a place for sitting and teaching.
aqsa.lm5_v1: An open structure on columns, without walls
aqsa.lm5_v2: Adjoining the Dome of the Rock to the east
aqsa.lm6_slotHint: Image of one of the mosque's minarets
aqsa.lm6_text: The mosque has four standing minarets: the Bab al-Asbat minaret to the north, the Bab al-Ghawanima minaret to the north-west, the Bab al-Silsila minaret to the west, and the Fakhriyya minaret to the south-west. Most were built in the Ayyubid and Mamluk eras.
aqsa.lm6_v1: Four minarets on the northern and western walls
aqsa.lm7_slotHint: Image of the mosque's arcades and learning platforms
aqsa.lm7_text: Stone arcades and vaults surround the Rock courtyard, and learning platforms are spread across the grounds, where teaching and memorisation circles have been held for centuries and are still used for lessons and retreat.
aqsa.lm7_v1: Study and memorisation circles, and gatherings of the murabitun
aqsa.lm7_v2: Around the Rock courtyard and across the grounds
aqsa.lm8_slotHint: Image of Qaytbay's fountain or the mosque's wells
aqsa.lm8_text: The mosque has thirty-seven wells collecting rainwater, and fountains for drinking and ablution, the most famous being the Mamluk-era Qaytbay Fountain west of the Rock courtyard, alongside the Cup Ablution Place between Al-Qibli and the Rock courtyard.
aqsa.lm8_v1: 37 wells · managed by the Jerusalem Waqf Department
aqsa.lm8_v2: Qaytbay Fountain · the Cup Ablution Place
aqsa.lm9_slotHint: Image of the schools surrounding the mosque
aqsa.lm9_text: Ayyubid and Mamluk-era schools, hospices and zawiyas surround the mosque to the north and west, built to serve students and residents; many today are homes for Jerusalemite families adjoining the mosque walls.
aqsa.tl1_text: Built forty years after the Sacred Mosque, its structure maintained successively by the prophets, peace be upon them.
aqsa.tl2_text: Umar ibn al-Khattab entered Jerusalem peacefully and gave its people the Umarid Covenant, securing them and their churches.
aqsa.tl3_title: Construction of the Dome of the Rock
aqsa.tl3_text: The Dome of the Rock was completed under Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, and Al-Qibli Prayer Hall was later built in the Umayyad era.
aqsa.tl4_text: Jerusalem was occupied and the mosque converted into a church and stable, lasting about ninety years.
aqsa.tl5_text: Saladin liberated Jerusalem after the Battle of Hattin, restored the mosque, and installed the minbar of Nur al-Din.
aqsa.tl6_text: Jerusalem's wall was renewed under Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, and the Dome of the Rock was faced with tiles.
aqsa.tl7_text: East Jerusalem, containing Al-Aqsa Mosque, was occupied, and the Maghariba Quarter adjoining the Western Wall was demolished.
aqsa.tl8_text: Fire was set in Al-Qibli Prayer Hall, consuming the historic minbar of Nur al-Din Zangi, later replaced.
aqsa.th1_text: Settler groups enter via Bab al-Maghariba under armed protection and perform rituals in our courtyards.
aqsa.th2_text: Attempts to allocate times and spaces inside the mosque to non-Muslims at the expense of worshippers.
aqsa.th3_text: Tunnels and excavations around and beneath it threaten its foundations and structure.
aqsa.th4_text: Barring categories of people from access, and expulsion orders against murabitun, staff and guards.
aqsa.th5_text: Obstruction of restoration work inside it, leaving damage in the buildings and arcades.
aqsa.th6_title: Emptying the surroundings of their people
aqsa.th6_text: Taxes and demolition and eviction orders against Old City residents to displace them from the mosque.
aqsa.heroAlt: A model of the blessed Al-Aqsa Mosque within its walls
aqsa.aerialAlt: Aerial view of Al-Aqsa Mosque within its wall
aqsa.minbarP1: The minbar of Al-Aqsa Mosque is among the rarest works ever crafted by human hands, and the most famous pulpit in history — not only for its bond with the mosque, but for the story of liberation in the time of Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi. For some eight hundred years it stood as a symbol of victory and dignity, from the day it was set in place until it was burned in 1969.
aqsa.minbarP2b: Ordered the finest craftsmen of Aleppo in 563 AH to build it in Damascus — twenty years before the liberation — so it would be placed in Al-Aqsa once the city was recovered. Nur al-Din died before seeing it in place, and after him came
aqsa.minbarP2c: Who liberated Bayt al-Maqdis on Friday 27 Rajab 583 AH and ordered the minbar brought and installed in the Qibli mosque.
aqsa.minbarP3b: Style: ornamental wooden pieces holding one another without a single nail or drop of glue, of wood inlaid with ivory and ebony, bearing Qur'anic and historical inscriptions — among them the verse “Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence” to the preacher's right as he ascends, Nur al-Din's name to his left, and the names of its makers on its door.
aqsa.mnHeightL: Its height, with a four-meter base and a one-meter-wide stair
aqsa.mnYearL: Made in Damascus by order of Nur al-Din Zangi
aqsa.mnFireL: The minbar and mosque were burned on 21 August
aqsa.fireWitnessPost: — preacher of Al-Aqsa Mosque and Custodian of the Minbar at Minbar Al Aqsa International Association, who examined the fire himself — says the perpetrators were more than one person acting under official cover: the fire broke out in several spots at once, using highly flammable materials unavailable to the public, and the primary target was the minbar, the symbol of the city's liberation. They came at seven in the morning when few people were present; the people of Al-Quds — men, women, elders and children — rushed to form lines passing earth and water, until fire engines arrived from Hebron, Bethlehem and Ramallah after the occupation authorities had obstructed their way.
aqsa.gatesLead: The mosque has gates in its northern and western walls; ten are open today, while the rest have been closed for centuries or were sealed later. The southern and eastern walls are entirely closed.
aqsa.custodyPre: Al-Aqsa Mosque is administered by the
aqsa.custodyAwqaf: Jerusalem Awqaf and Al-Aqsa Mosque Affairs Department
aqsa.custodyPost: , the body responsible for restoration, maintenance, study circles and the guards, working under the Hashemite custodianship of the holy sites in Al-Quds. Everything published on this page about the mosque's area, landmarks and wells is based on its data and official guide.

homepage.faq1Q: Is the calculator a religious ruling?
homepage.faq1A: No. It is an estimate based on the values you enter. Consult a trusted religious authority to confirm whether Zakat is due and how much.
homepage.faq2Q: Does Zakat stay separate from other donations?
homepage.faq2A: Yes. The donation type appears as Zakat in the cart and on the receipt, and it is spent only on Zakat-eligible projects.
homepage.faq3Q: What is the Zakat rate and how is it calculated?
homepage.faq3A: 2.5% of net zakatable wealth after deducting due liabilities, once it reaches the nisab and a lunar year has passed.
homepage.faq4Q: What is the difference between Waqf and Sadaqah?
homepage.faq4A: Sadaqah is spent directly on its purpose, while Waqf is tied to a project or asset whose benefit continues by its nature.
homepage.faq5Q: When do I receive the Waqf certificate?
homepage.faq5A: The certificate is issued after payment completes and the details are reviewed and approved, in the name of the donor or the dedicatee.
homepage.faq6Q: Can the Waqf be in someone else's name?
homepage.faq6A: Yes. Enter the name of the donor or dedicatee and a dedication message; they appear on the certificate as you wrote them.
homepage.faq7A: Payment goes through an approved gateway, and an official receipt with the amount and intention follows.
homepage.faq8Q: Can I change or stop a recurring donation?

homepage.faq9A: Yes. Choose the currency at the top of the page; the amount is converted at payment.

jerusalem.heroLead: Our city, guarded by its people simply by staying. Here are its walls, gates, quarters and landmarks — what is being done to it today, and what we do alongside its people.
jerusalem.wallBuiltBy: The wall standing today was built by Sultan
jerusalem.wallDetails: Between 1535 and 1542. It runs about 4.3 kilometres, stands ten to fifteen metres high, and carries thirty-five towers — most of them along the northern wall, the most exposed to attack.
jerusalem.newGateDetails: , opened in 1887 under Sultan Abdulhamid II to ease entry for the city's people and the neighbouring villages. It was closed in 1948 and later reopened.
jerusalem.stayingText: Every Jerusalemite home restored, every family that stays within the walls, means the city still belongs to its people. Emptying the Old City of its residents is the aim; staying is the answer.
jerusalem.quarterJewishNote: (formerly Harat al-Sharaf and the Moroccan Quarter)
jerusalem.quartersLead: An old division of the walled city — its boundaries are connected alleys and markets, not barriers.
jerusalem.gatesLead: Seven open gates through which the city's people and visitors pass, and the Golden Gate in the east, sealed for centuries. Each gate is a name on the tongues of Jerusalemites before it is a mark on a map.
jerusalem.seeOnMap: See their locations on the map
jerusalem.landmarksLead: Mosques, markets, schools and water fountains — and a quarter erased from the map but not from memory.
jerusalem.mapCaption: The four quarters, the gates and the landmarks within the walls. A drawing to introduce the locations, not a surveyed plan.
jerusalem.whatIsWanted: What is intended for our Old City

waqf.goal1: To sustain support and funding for projects inside Al-Aqsa Mosque — study circles, memorisation and recitation classes, scholars' chairs, iftars and youth activities — and for restoration and building work across Al-Quds, especially the Old City, strengthening the resilience of its people, the first shield protecting Al-Aqsa against the harshest living conditions the occupation imposes to empty the city of its residents.

waqf.meterIntro: Symbolic in name, far-reaching in effect: sustainable endowments generating a yield that serves Al-Aqsa, protects its Islamic identity and keeps its people steadfast.
waqf.whatIsWaqfText: Waqf is an ongoing charity by which wealth passes out of its owner's possession into God's; it is not sold, gifted or inherited. The asset remains preserved so its yield can be spent continuously on the field dedicated to it. Your endowment in the square-metre or share project keeps its effect for as long as the projects of Al-Quds and Al-Aqsa endure, God willing.
waqf.aidTypesText: The yield of the square-metre and share project is spent on approved areas that directly serve Al-Aqsa and the people of Al-Quds, chief among them:
waqf.partsText: The project is designed to cover the areas of spending that serve Al-Aqsa, the holy sites and the causes of Al-Quds, achieving a lasting and sustainable impact.
waqf.ctaHeading: Take your share of reward in Al-Quds
waqf.ctaText: Take part in the Waqf project — your endowment's giving remains a lasting mark.
waqf.meterText1: The Waqf square metre is symbolic in name yet weighty in effect: it seeks to establish sustainable endowments that generate sufficient funds and suitable yield to serve Al-Aqsa Mosque, protect it, affirm its Islamic character and keep steadfast the people who stand guard there — those who act on behalf of the ummah through their defence, patience and resolve, giving what is dearest to preserve the dignity of all Muslims and safeguard their sanctuaries. This is done by dividing the area of Al-Aqsa symbolically and figuratively into square metres, then apportioning the material cost each square metre requires to remain Islamic, alive and steadfast — through many projects: memorisation circles, study benches, iftar tables, lessons of knowledge, drinking-water provision, and student and community activities, among others.
waqf.meterText2: After careful study and extensive data-gathering on the holy city and its Al-Aqsa Mosque, the financial cost of each square metre was assessed at about $1,500, invested in a sustainable Waqf project whose yield goes to guarding Al-Aqsa. By God's grace the square-metre project has begun to bear fruit: the Rightly-Guided Caliphs Waqf Complex in Sur Baher, Al-Quds — the city's largest Islamic complex after Al-Aqsa itself — opened in March 2022; and a set of licensed, legally established investment projects in Istanbul now returns its yield to serving Al-Aqsa.
waqf.meterText3: To make giving easier and widen the door of reward for all, we divided the square-metre project so a donor may split a metre into fifteen parts and give what they can — this became the Waqf share. A share costs $100 and is spent on the same Waqf projects by the same mechanism as the square metre, and Minber issues the donor an official, attested certificate.

zakat.faq_hawl_q: How do I determine the Zakat year (hawl)?
zakat.faq_hawl_a: The hawl is one full lunar year during which the wealth stays in your possession at or above the nisab. Fix one Hijri date for yourself and calculate on it every year.
zakat.faq_metal_q: Which should I choose: the gold or silver nisab?
zakat.faq_metal_a: The silver nisab is lower in value, so using it is more cautious and more beneficial to the poor, since it obligates Zakat on less wealth. Many scholars today favor it.
zakat.faq_salary_q: Do I pay Zakat on my monthly salary?
zakat.faq_salary_a: Zakat is on what remains of it, enters your savings, and completes a full year — not on the salary at the moment you receive it.
zakat.faq_jewelry_q: How do I pay Zakat on a wife's jewelry?
zakat.faq_jewelry_a: Those who hold that used jewelry is zakatable pay on its weight every year. Enter the weight by karat in the calculator, and consult someone whose knowledge you trust.
zakat.faq_early_q: Is it permissible to pay Zakat early?
zakat.faq_early_a: The majority of scholars permit paying it early before the year is complete when there is a clear need, which fits the situation of our people in Gaza and Al-Quds.
zakat.faq_channels_q: Does my Zakat reach only its prescribed categories?
zakat.faq_channels_a: Yes. Zakat is kept separate from other donations, spent only on its prescribed categories, and this appears on the receipt.

zakat.whyText: The people of Palestine face continuous measures targeting them, which have worsened their economic situation, driving poverty to 80% and unemployment to 30%. At Minbar Al Aqsa International Association, we make sure Zakat funds reach them, easing their burden and helping them remain on their land.
zakat.rewardText: When you give your Zakat to Palestine, the blessing of giving Zakat joins the blessing of the holy land, and you earn a double reward.
zakat.masarifIntro: We distribute Zakat strictly within its prescribed categories, as stated in the words of Allah Almighty:
zakat.testimonial1Quote: Most of the eight categories mentioned in verse 60 of Surat At-Tawbah are present among the people of Palestine, and Al-Quds in particular; every effort must be made, by all means, to support the people of Al-Quds in remaining steadfast on their land.
zakat.expediteText: The Prophet (peace be upon him) permitted Al-Abbas to pay his Zakat early. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said to Umar: 'We took Al-Abbas's Zakat for this year in the previous year.' Most scholars hold that paying Zakat early is permissible, from one month up to more than two years.
zakat.testimonial2Quote: Sheikh Ikrima Sabri, Mufti of Al-Aqsa Mosque, issued a fatwa on the necessity of expediting Zakat for the people of Palestine — especially Al-Quds and Gaza — given the urgent need afflicting the poor and needy due to the city's suffering, ongoing for more than seven decades.

zenki.heroTitle: The Nur ad-Din Mahmud Zangi Course
zenki.heroLead: A comprehensive academic course on the cause of Bayt al-Maqdis and Al-Aqsa Mosque, delivered in nine units of knowledge and values, with a supplementary annex for preachers and callers.
zenki.introText1: This is a Jerusalem-focused knowledge programme aimed at equipping preachers to convey knowledge and build Jerusalem awareness among the Umma's public, students of knowledge, and those active in serving its causes.
zenki.introText2: The programme does not aim merely to impart abstract information, but to make the preacher a more effective agent in spreading awareness and knowledge of the cause of Bayt al-Maqdis — after equipping him with the essential grounding to understand the cause and its historical, legal and practical dimensions — and to convey this awareness to the wider Umma through his various preaching platforms.
